title: Reference
text: This page summarizes the main functions described in the VedicDateTime paper. Function names below reflect the paper’s Tables and listings.

title: Reference
text:
Core pattern
Many functions follow the pattern:

Input:

jd — Julian Day Number
place — numeric vector: c(latitude, longitude, timezone)

Output:

an index (which entity)
ending time as (hour, minute, second)


The paper shows this output style for tithi, nakshatra, yoga, etc.

title: Reference
text:
Panchanga: five core entities

tithi() / tithis()
Purpose: compute the tithi (lunar day) at sunrise and its end time; may return two tithis in special cases.
Paper example:
jd <- 2459778
place <- c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5)

tithi(jd, place)
#> [1] 20 20 55 35
Related helper:

get_tithi_name() — map tithi number to name.



vaara() / vaaras()
Purpose: Vedic weekday.
Paper examples:
vaara(2459778)
#> [1] 1

get_vaara_name(2459778)
#> [1] "Ravivar"


nakshatra() / nakshatras()
Purpose: compute nakshatra from the moon’s sidereal longitude.
Notes from the paper:

uses Lahiri Ayanamsa
sunrise/time calculations via Swiss Ephemeris
end times via Inverse Lagrange interpolation with 0.25 day offsets

Example:
nakshatra(2459778, c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5))
#> [1] 25 24 24  1


yoga() / yogas()
Purpose: 27 yogas derived from sun and moon longitudes (segment size 13°20′).
Example:
yoga(2459778, c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5))
#> [1]  5 27 26 12


karana() / karanas()
Purpose: half-tithi (recurring + fixed karanas).
Example:
karana(2459778, c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5))
#> [1] 39 40

get_karana_name(39, 40)
#> [1] "Kaulava-Taitila"

title: VedicDateTime
text:
VedicDateTime is an open-source R package that implements key components of the Vedic calendar (lunisolar) and provides conversions from Gregorian date-time (or Julian Day Number) to Vedic calendar entities.
The motivation is that many phenomena—especially in time-series analysis—can be influenced by both solar and lunar cycles. The package paper presents VedicDateTime and demonstrates two applied case studies using the package.
Get started Reference

title: VedicDateTime
text:
What does the package compute?
VedicDateTime implements the core parts of Panchanga (“five arms” of the Vedic calendar):

Tithi — lunar day (phase-based)
Vaara — weekday
Nakshatra — constellation segment based on the moon’s position
Yoga — derived from sun + moon longitudes
Karana — half-tithi

The package also includes additional related entities and utilities (see Reference), such as:

sunrise/sunset, moonrise/moonset
solar/lunar longitudes
rashi, lagna, masa, ritu, samvatsara
Gregorian ↔︎ Julian day conversion helpers

title: VedicDateTime
text:
Why a lunisolar calendar?
Calendar systems can be solar, lunar, or lunisolar. The Gregorian calendar is a solar calendar and serves as a modern standard. However, Vedic calendars are lunisolar and can be useful when the analysis depends on the dynamics of both the sun and the moon.
The VedicDateTime paper motivates use in calendar seasonality and moving-holiday effects (e.g., festivals whose timing shifts under the Gregorian calendar).

title: VedicDateTime
text:
Quick example (from the paper)
Below is an example shown in the package paper (note: code is displayed; it is not executed when building this site).
# Julian day number
jd <- 2459778

# Latitude, Longitude, and timezone of the location
place <- c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5)

tithi(jd, place)
#> [1] 20 20 55 35
Interpretation (as explained in the paper):

The first number is the tithi index (there are 30 tithis).
The remaining values indicate the ending time (hour, minute, second) for that tithi.

title: VedicDateTime
text:
Scope and outputs
Many functions return compact numeric vectors that include:

an index (e.g., which tithi/nakshatra/yoga)
the end time for the current entity (hour/minute/second)

In some situations, two entities can occur on one date, and the output may include both (e.g., two tithis with their end times). The paper also notes handling of skipped/leap cases.

Implementation notes (from the paper)
The paper describes algorithmic elements such as:

Calculations anchored to sunrise for a specified location
Use of Lahiri Ayanamsa (sidereal correction)
Use of Swiss Ephemeris (via R dependencies) for astronomical quantities
Determining end times using Inverse Lagrange interpolation with 0.25 day offsets

title: Articles
text: This section expands on the motivations and examples described in the VedicDateTime paper.

title: Articles
text:
Background: calendar systems and time-series
The paper motivates VedicDateTime by noting that calendars can be solar, lunar, or lunisolar.

Gregorian calendar: solar (commonly used as a modern time reference)
Vedic calendar: lunisolar (based on both sun and moon motions)

A key idea in the paper is that some natural and social processes can exhibit patterns aligned with lunar and solar cycles, and that using a lunisolar calendar can sometimes make those patterns easier to model.

title: Articles
text:
Panchanga (five arms)
The paper uses the term Panchanga (five arms):

Tithi (lunar day)
Vaara (weekday)
Nakshatra (constellation segment)
Yoga
Karana (half-tithi)

VedicDateTime implements these entities and provides conversions from Gregorian/Julian dates.

title: Articles
section: Case study 1 — Calendar seasonality in economic output
text:
Case study 1 — Calendar seasonality in economic output
The paper presents a case study on India’s Index of Industrial Production (IIP) to illustrate “calendar seasonality” effects.
High-level workflow described:

Start with a time series indexed by Gregorian dates.
Convert dates to Vedic calendar entities using VedicDateTime.
Analyze seasonality (the paper discusses decomposition approaches and comparisons).

title: Articles
section: Case study 2 — Diwali regressors (moving holiday effects)
text:
Case study 2 — Diwali regressors (moving holiday effects)
The paper also discusses Diwali as an example of a moving festival whose Gregorian timing shifts year-to-year.
High-level workflow described:

Identify Diwali dates and/or Vedic-calendar markers.
Create regressors (indicator variables) around the festival period.
Fit a time-series model / seasonal adjustment approach.

The motivation is that such effects can be hard to capture with fixed Gregorian calendar features alone.

title: Getting started
text:
Key inputs: time + place
Most VedicDateTime computations use:

A date expressed as a Julian Day Number (JD)
A place vector containing:

latitude
longitude
timezone offset


This is stated repeatedly in the paper examples (e.g., place <- c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5)).

Convert Gregorian date → Julian day
The paper describes gregorian_to_jd() as the helper to convert a Gregorian date to a Julian day.
# Example (paper shows this pattern)
# jd <- gregorian_to_jd(day, month, year)

title: Getting started
text:
Your first Panchanga computation

1) Tithi
From the paper:

tithi(jd, place) calculates the tithi for a given Julian day and place.
It determines the tithi at sunrise, based on the difference between lunar and solar longitudes divided by 12.
The ending time is computed using Inverse Lagrange interpolation using longitudes at 0.25 day intervals from sunrise.

Example (from the paper):
jd <- 2459778
place <- c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5)

tithi(jd, place)
#> [1] 20 20 55 35
What the output means:

first value = tithi index (1..30)
next three values = end time (hour, minute, second)

If you see times beyond 24:00, it indicates a time past midnight (next day), as explained in the paper.


2) Vaara (weekday)
vaara(2459778)
#> [1] 1

get_vaara_name(2459778)
#> [1] "Ravivar"


3) Nakshatra
From the paper, nakshatra() is computed from the moon’s position:

moon’s sidereal (Nirayana) longitude is found by subtracting Ayanamsa from tropical longitude
the paper states the package uses Lahiri Ayanamsa and obtains sunrise via Swiss Ephemeris
end times use Inverse Lagrange interpolation with 0.25 day offsets

Example output shown:
jd <- 2459778
place <- c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5)

nakshatra(jd, place)
#> [1] 25 24 24  1
The paper explains this as nakshatra index + ending time.


4) Yoga
The paper notes 27 yogas, calculated from sun and moon longitudes, using a 13°20′ segment size.
yoga(2459778, c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5))
#> [1]  5 27 26 12


5) Karana
The paper describes karana as half-tithi and notes both “fixed” and “recurring” karanas.
karana(2459778, c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5))
#> [1] 39 40

get_karana_name(39, 40)
#> [1] "Kaulava-Taitila"

title: Getting started
text:
Common mistakes

Package not installed: if you see there is no package called 'VedicDateTime', install from CRAN (or GitHub) before running library(VedicDateTime).
Website builds failing: this website is configured to not execute code chunks during rendering (so examples can be shown even if the package is not installed).
Timezone mismatch: use the correct timezone offset for the chosen latitude/longitude.

title: VedicDateTime website (GitHub Pages)
text:
This folder contains a Quarto website intended to be published with GitHub Pages.



Install Quarto: https://quarto.org/
In RStudio (or terminal), from this folder:

quarto preview



quarto render
This renders the site to docs/ (configured in _quarto.yml).



Recommended approach for a project site:

Commit the website source files and the generated docs/ folder to your default branch (e.g., main).
In GitHub repo → Settings → Pages:

Source: Deploy from a branch
Branch: main
Folder: /docs

Save. GitHub will publish at:

https://<OWNER>.github.io/<REPO>/






Choose a domain, e.g. vedicdatetime.example.com.
In GitHub repo → Settings → Pages → Custom domain:

Enter your domain and save.

DNS configuration (typical):

For a subdomain (vedicdatetime.example.com): create a CNAME record pointing to <OWNER>.github.io.
For an apex domain (example.com): use A records to GitHub Pages IPs (see GitHub docs).

Create docs/CNAME containing exactly your domain name on one line.

Start by copying CNAME.template → docs/CNAME and editing it.

(Recommended) Enable Enforce HTTPS in GitHub Pages settings after DNS propagates.

Run quarto render and commit the generated docs/ folder
GitHub → Settings → Pages → Branch: main and folder /docs
Confirm all links work on the published URL





Update _quarto.yml with:

website.repo-url
